Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space. A complex Borel measure $\mu$
on $X$ is **regular** if its total variation
$|\mu|$ is a regular Borel measure in the preceding, all-Borel sense. This
total-variation convention is the one that controls $|\int f\,d\mu|$ and the
norm in the $C_0$ representation theorem.

For this page, a Borel measure $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff space is
**Radon** when $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact $K$, and, for every Borel
$E$ and every open $U$,
$$\mu(E)=\inf_{E\subseteq V\text{ open}}\mu(V),\qquad \mu(U)=\sup_{K\subseteq U\text{ compact}}\mu(K).$$
Cohn calls this convention regular. It does not assert compact inner
approximation for arbitrary Borel $E$.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The real numbers) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).

   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$

time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Then
$|\nu|$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

A **regular Borel measure** here is a Radon measure $\mu$ for which every
Borel $E$ satisfies $\mu(E)=\sup_{K\subseteq E,\ K\text{ compact}}\mu(K)$,
with equality allowed at $+\infty$. Thus regularity strengthens the preceding

derivations.claim: For every Borel $A$ and every countable Borel partition $(A_j)$ of $A$, the Euclidean norm satisfies $|\mu(A_j)|\le\sum_{i=1}^m|\mu_i(A_j)|$. Summing over $j$ gives $V(A)\le\lambda(A)$ for $\lambda:=\sum_{i=1}^m|\mu_i|$, so $V$ is finite and $V(\Omega)<\infty$.

If $A=\bigsqcup_{k\ge1}E_k$ is a disjoint Borel union, then intersecting any partition of $A$ with each $E_k$ and using countable additivity of each coordinate shows $V(A)\le\sum_kV(E_k)$. Conversely, for fixed $N$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose for each of the finitely many $k\le N$ a partition of $E_k$ whose sum exceeds $V(E_k)-\varepsilon/N$. Their union, together with $A\setminus\bigcup_{k\le N}E_k$, is a partition of $A$, so $V(A)\ge\sum_{k\le N}V(E_k)-\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and then $N\to\infty$ proves countable additivity. Thus $V$ is a finite positive Borel measure.

For every $f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$ with $|f|\le1$, approximate $f$ uniformly by finite-valued Borel simple functions whose values have norm at most one. The partition definition bounds each simple integral by $V(\Omega)$, and finiteness of the coordinate measures lets the uniform errors tend to zero. Hence the displayed supremum is at most $V(\Omega)$.

Since $V\le\lambda$ and $\lambda=\sum_i|\mu_i|$ is a finite regular Borel measure by [F1], for every Borel $A$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\lambda(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$, whence $V(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$. There is also an open $G\supseteq A$ with $\lambda(G\setminus A)<\varepsilon$, whence $V(G\setminus A)<\varepsilon$. Thus $V$ is a regular Borel measure in the sense of [[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]], and in particular a Radon measure.

If $V(\Omega)=0$, the zero field proves the reverse inequality. Otherwise fix $0<\varepsilon<V(\Omega)/4$ and choose a countable Borel partition $(A_j)$ with sum greater than $V(\Omega)-\varepsilon$; truncate after $N\ge1$ so the tail is below $\varepsilon$. Omit indices with $\mu(A_j)=0$ or $V(A_j)\le\varepsilon/(4N)$; the sum of the omitted partition values is at most $\varepsilon/4$. For every retained index, compact inner regularity [F2] gives a nonempty compact $K_j\subset A_j$ with $V(A_j\setminus K_j)<\varepsilon/(8N)$. Since there are finitely many pairwise disjoint compact sets $K_j$ in the metric space $\Omega$, choose pairwise disjoint open neighborhoods $N_j$ with compact closures in $\Omega$. Outer regularity [F2] gives open $G_j\supset K_j$ with $V(G_j\setminus K_j)<\varepsilon/(8N)$. Put $U_j=G_j\cap N_j$. Then $K_j\subset U_j$, $V(U_j\setminus K_j)<\varepsilon/(8N)$, and the closures of the $U_j$ remain pairwise disjoint compact subsets of $\Omega$. Define $$\psi_j(x):=\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,\Omega\setminus U_j)}{\operatorname{dist}(x,\Omega\setminus U_j)+\operatorname{dist}(x,K_j)}.$$ This is continuous and compactly supported, equals one on $K_j$, and vanishes outside $U_j$. Set $e_j=\mu(A_j)/|\mu(A_j)|$ and $f=\sum_j e_j\psi_j$. The disjoint closures of the $U_j$ imply disjoint supports and $|f|\le1$. For bounded Borel vector fields, the partition definition and uniform simple-function approximation give $|\int g\cdot d\mu|\le\int|g|\,dV$. Thus replacing $e_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ by $e_j\psi_j$ loses at most $V(A_j\setminus K_j)+V(U_j\setminus K_j)$ for each retained $j$. Summing these errors, the omitted terms, and the tail gives $\int f\cdot d\mu>V(\Omega)-3\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the reverse bound.

derivations.claim: If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the empty family proves the claim. Otherwise, for $m\ge1$ set $K_m=\{x:|x|\le m,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,\Omega^c)\ge1/m\}$ when $\Omega\ne\mathbb R^n$, and set $K_m=\overline B(0,m)$ when $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$; put $K_m=\varnothing$ for $m\le0$. Each $K_m$ is compact by [F1], the sets are nested, $K_m\subset\operatorname{int}K_{m+1}$, and their interiors cover $\Omega$. The compact shells $S_m:=K_m\setminus\operatorname{int}K_{m-1}$ cover $\Omega$ and lie in the open sets $U_m:=\operatorname{int}K_{m+1}\setminus K_{m-2}$. The family $(U_m)$ is locally finite: any compact subset of $\Omega$ lies in some $\operatorname{int}K_N$ and hence in $K_{m-2}$ for all sufficiently large $m$.

Fix once a smooth nonnegative cutoff $\theta$ equal to one on $\overline B(0,1)$ and supported in $B(0,2)$, whose existence is [F3]. In each $U_m$, consider the rational inner balls $B(q,r)$ for which $\overline B(q,2r)\subset U_m\cap V_\ell$ for some cover index $\ell$. Indexed by $(\ell,q,r)$, these balls form a countable cover of $S_m$: for each point choose a cover member containing it, then density [F2] gives a rational center and radius with the required doubled closure. Compactness of $S_m$ gives a finite subcover. Order all finite lists of eligible indexed balls by natural-number codes and take the first list covering $S_m$; thus no choice principle is needed. Its sum $s:=\sum_{m,j}\psi_{m,j}$ is smooth and positive on $\Omega$ because the shells cover $\Omega$.

Define $\eta_{m,j}:=\psi_{m,j}/s$. Then each function is smooth, nonnegative and compactly supported in $\Omega$, the family is locally finite, and $\sum_{m,j}\eta_{m,j}=1$. Each support remains in its assigned cover member, and enumeration gives the required countable family.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

- A **separation** of $X$ is an ordered pair $(U, V)$ of **open**, **nonempty**,
  **disjoint** subsets of $X$ with $U \cup V = X$.
- $X$ is **disconnected** when a separation of $X$ exists, and **connected** when
  none does.
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **connected subset** of $X$ when the space
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is connected, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the subspace topology
  ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). "Disconnected subset" is read the same way.

Since $U$ and $V$ are complementary in $X$, each of them is closed as well as
open; so a separation is the same thing as a partition of $X$ into two nonempty
clopen pieces ([[def-topological-space]]). The **clopen** subsets of $X$ are
those that are both open and closed, and $\varnothing$ and $X$ are always among
them.

**The empty space and the one-point space are connected in this library.**
Neither admits a separation: a separation requires two nonempty disjoint sets
whose union is the whole space, and neither $\varnothing$ nor a singleton can be
written as such a union. So both are connected under the definition above,
without any special clause. **This is a live convention fork** and the competing
choice is recorded in [[rem-connectedness-conventions]]; nothing on this page
depends on which is taken except the reading of the word "connected" applied to
those two spaces.

**Connectedness is a property of a space, not of an ambient pair.** The condition
above mentions only $(X,\mathcal{T})$. When it is applied to $A \subseteq X$ it
is applied to the space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$, so it does not change if $A$ is
regarded as a subspace of some other space inducing the same topology on $A$; in
particular a subset of $A$ is connected as a subset of $A$ exactly when it is
connected as a subset of $X$, by transitivity of the subspace topology
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). This is why "connected" may be used of a subset
with no ambient space named.

**Spelled out for a subset.** $A \subseteq X$ is disconnected exactly when there
are open $U, V \subseteq X$ with

$$A \subseteq U \cup V, \qquad U \cap A \ne \varnothing, \qquad V \cap A \ne \varnothing, \qquad U \cap V \cap A = \varnothing,$$

because the open sets of $(A,\mathcal{T}_A)$ are precisely the traces $U \cap A$.
Note the last condition: it asks $U$ and $V$ to be disjoint **on $A$**, not in
$X$. Requiring $U \cap V = \varnothing$ outright is a strictly stronger demand
and is a different notion.

**The two-point discrete space.** Write $\mathbf{2} := \{0,1\}$ with the discrete
topology ([[def-standard-topologies]]), in which every subset is open. A
separation of $X$ is the same datum as a surjective continuous map
$X \to \mathbf{2}$ ([[def-continuous-map-top]]): given $(U,V)$, the map sending
$U$ to $0$ and $V$ to $1$ is continuous because the preimage of each of the four
open subsets of $\mathbf{2}$ is one of $\varnothing$, $U$, $V$, $X$; given a
surjective continuous $\chi : X \to \mathbf{2}$, the pair
$(\chi^{-1}[\{0\}], \chi^{-1}[\{1\}])$ is a separation. This reformulation is
proved as a theorem on this page and is recorded here only to name $\mathbf{2}$.

$$\overline{A_1} \cap A_2 = \varnothing \qquad \text{and} \qquad A_1 \cap \overline{A_2} = \varnothing,$$

$A_1 \subseteq \overline{A_1}$; the converse fails. This is verbatim the
condition [[def-connected-r]] uses on the real line, transported to an arbitrary
space, and the theorem relating it to the definition above is the next lemma on
this page.

all of whose connected subsets are single points is fixed later on this page,
together with the components; it is not defined here because it is stated in
terms of components.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$
using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m)$ have finite signed Radon coordinate measures. For Borel $A\subseteq\Omega$ define $$V(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |\mu(A_j)|:(A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$ where the norm is Euclidean. Then $V$ is a finite positive Radon measure and $$V(\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega f\cdot d\mu:f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^m),\ |f(x)|\le1\right\}.$$

Let $X$ be locally compact Hausdorff and let $f:X\to\mathbb F$ be continuous,
where $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. Its support is
$\operatorname{supp}f:=\overline{\{x:f(x)\ne0\}}$. Put
$C_c(X;\mathbb F)=\{f\in C(X;\mathbb F):\operatorname{supp}f\text{ is compact}\}$.
Also $C_0(X;\mathbb F)$ consists of those $f$ for which, for every $\epsilon>0$,
$\{x:|f(x)|\ge\epsilon\}$ is compact. We write $C_c(X)$ for the real space
until the bounded complex $C_0$ theorem is invoked; $C_0(X)$ later means the
complex space when its scalar field matters.
For every open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, the space $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in $C_0(\Omega)$ in the uniform norm.

Assume Countable Choice. For every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, every bounded real linear functional on $C_0(U;\mathbb R)$ is integration against a unique finite signed Radon measure. No Dependent Choice assumption is required.

derivations.claim: Suppose $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and write $\mu=Du$. The distributional derivative identity gives $\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx=-\int_\Omega\varphi\cdot d\mu$. The continuous-field dual formula [F2] bounds the supremum over smooth fields by $|\mu|(\Omega)$. Conversely, for any $f\in C_c(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$ with $|f|\le1$, for every $\varepsilon>0$, density [F3] gives one smooth compactly supported $g$ with $\|g-f\|_\infty<\varepsilon$; replacing $g$ by $g/\max(1,\|g\|_\infty)$ keeps the unit bound and changes this error by at most another $\varepsilon$. Finiteness of the coordinate measures bounds the integral error by a fixed constant times $\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ (without selecting a sequence of approximants) shows that the smooth supremum is at least the continuous-field supremum $|\mu|(\Omega)$. Thus $V(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$.

Assume [A1], let real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$, and suppose $M:=V(u)<\infty$. For each coordinate $i$, define $L_i(\psi):=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\psi\,dx$ on real $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Taking the test vector with only its $i$th component equal to $\psi$ and also its negative shows $|L_i(\psi)|\le M\|\psi\|_\infty$. By density [F3], $L_i$ extends uniquely to a bounded real linear functional on real $C_0(\Omega)$. Apply [F4] directly to this real functional to obtain a finite signed Radon measure $\mu_i$ representing $D_i u$. Applying [F2] to $\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n)$ and using [F3] to pass between continuous and smooth unit fields gives $|\mu|(\Omega)=M$. Hence $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $TV(u;\Omega)=M$.

If the $L^1$ limit $u$ is already in $BV(\Omega)$, boundedness of $\operatorname{div}\varphi$ gives $\int u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi=\lim_k\int u_k\,\operatorname{div}\varphi$ for each admissible $\varphi$. Each approximating integral is at most $TV(u_k;\Omega)$ by step 1.1, so taking the supremum gives $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$; this branch uses no choice axiom.

If only $L:=\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)<\infty$ is known, choose a subsequence whose variations converge to $L$. The same test-integral limit gives $V(u)\le L$. Under [A1], step 1.2 implies $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $TV(u;\Omega)=V(u)\le L$. If $L=+\infty$, the extended inequality is automatic.

Let $n\ge1$ and assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Lebesgue measure on
$\mathbb R^n$ is a Radon measure, and it is regular in the stronger

An **$L^1$ approximate identity** on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a family
$(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of functions in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where

$$\|K_\varepsilon\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx,$$

such that:

1. $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} K_\varepsilon(x)\,dx = 1$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$;
2. there is $M < \infty$ with $\|K_\varepsilon\|_1 \le M$ for every
   $\varepsilon > 0$;
3. for every $\delta > 0$,
   $$ \int_{|x|>\delta} |K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

This is the general notion used later for both compactly supported mollifiers
and the Gaussian family.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and $r\ge1$ be integers, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^r$ map with

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $h:Q\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Then $h$ is differentiable almost everywhere, its partial derivatives are measurable and are its weak derivatives. On every open region where $h$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $|Dh|\le L$ almost everywhere. Let $H^m$ denote the repository's unnormalised Hausdorff measure, put $c_m=H^m((0,1]^m)$, and write $\sigma_m=c_m^{-1}H^m$ also on Euclidean spaces containing $m$-dimensional subsets. The graph map $F(y)=(y,h(y))$ satisfies, for every nonnegative Borel $a$,
$$\int_{F(Q)}a(x)\,d\sigma_m(x)=\int_Qa(F(y))\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}\,dy.$$
For the epigraph $G=\{(y,z):y\in Q,\ z>h(y)\}$, a smooth vector field compactly supported away from the chart sides satisfies
$$\int_G\operatorname{div}\phi\,dx=\int_Q\phi(y,h(y))\cdot(Dh(y),-1)\,dy.$$
Thus its outward normal is $(Dh,-1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ almost everywhere. The sign reverses for a subgraph. The graph surface measure is locally finite and Radon on $F(Q)$ with its relative topology, and its null sets coincide with graph images of Lebesgue-null subsets of the base.

Then $0\le p(G)\le\|P\|$, $p(\varnothing)=0$, and $p$ is monotone. If a compact $K$ is covered by open sets $G_j$, finitely many suffice, and there are continuous nonnegative compactly supported functions $b_1,\ldots,b_N$, each supported in one of these sets, whose sum is positive on $K$. Indeed cover $K$ by finitely many balls with doubled closures compactly contained in the relevant $G_j$ and use distance cutoffs on these balls. On a neighborhood of $K$ normalize the $b_i$ by their sum. Thus any $f$ supported on $K$ with $0\le f\le1$ decomposes into finitely many $f_i\ge0$ with $\sum f_i=f$ and each $f_i\le1$ compactly supported in its assigned $G_j$; combine terms assigned to the same $j$. Consequently $p(\bigcup_jG_j)\le\sum_jp(G_j)$. For pairwise disjoint opens, adding finitely many admissible functions gives the reverse inequality for every finite partial sum, so $p$ is countably additive on disjoint open unions. These compact partitions use only finite choices.

Define $\mu^*(A)=\inf\{p(G):A\subseteq G\subseteq U,\ G\text{ open}\}$. For a sequence $(A_j)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [A1] selects open $G_j\supseteq A_j$ with $p(G_j)<\mu^*(A_j)+\varepsilon2^{-j}$; step 1.1 proves countable subadditivity. Zero and monotonicity are immediate, so $\mu^*$ is an outer measure, and $\mu^*(G)=p(G)$ for open $G$. If $\operatorname{dist}(A,B)>0$, they have disjoint open neighborhoods $V,W$ in $U$. Every open $G\supseteq A\cup B$ satisfies $p(G)\ge p(G\cap V)+p(G\cap W)\ge\mu^*(A)+\mu^*(B)$, by step 1.1. Taking the infimum and using subadditivity proves the metric condition. By [F2], restriction to Borel sets is a finite measure $\mu$ with $\mu(U)\le\|P\|$.

For an admissible $f$ in the definition of $p(G)$, let $K=\operatorname{supp}f$. Every open $V\supseteq K$ admits $f$, hence $\mu(K)=\inf_{V\supseteq K}p(V)\ge P(f)$. Taking the supremum over $f$ proves $\mu(G)=\sup_{K\subseteq G\text{ compact}}\mu(K)$. Outer regularity on every Borel set is the definition of $\mu^*$. Finiteness gives compact inner regularity on every Borel set as well: given Borel $A$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose compact $H\subseteq U$ with $\mu(U\setminus H)<\varepsilon$ and open $V\supseteq U\setminus A$ with $\mu(V\setminus(U\setminus A))<\varepsilon$. Then $H\setminus V\subseteq A$ is compact and misses at most $2\varepsilon$ of $\mu(A)$. Thus $\mu$ is finite Radon, including regularity on all Borel sets.

If $0\le g\in C_c(U)$ and $g\le\mathbf1_K$ for compact $K$, the argument in step 3.1 gives $P(g)\le\mu(K)$. If instead $g\ge\mathbf1_K$, then for $0<\eta<1$, the open set $G_\eta=\{g>1-\eta\}$ contains $K$ and every admissible $f$ for $p(G_\eta)$ satisfies $f\le g/(1-\eta)$ on all of $U$. Positivity yields $\mu(K)\le p(G_\eta)\le P(g)/(1-\eta)$. Letting $\eta\downarrow0$ gives $\mu(K)\le P(g)$.

Fix $0\le f\in C_c(U)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, take $N$ with $N\varepsilon\ge\|f\|_\infty$, and put $f_j=\min(\varepsilon,(f-(j-1)\varepsilon)_+)$, $K_0=\operatorname{supp}f$, $K_j=\{f\ge j\varepsilon\}$ for $1\le j\le N$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x

$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ is the completion of the product measure

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Thus, writing $\omega(r)=\sup_{k,|h|\le r}\|v_k(\cdot+h)-v_k\|_1$, one has $\sup_k\|v_k-A_\delta v_k\|_1\le2^n\omega(\sqrt n\delta)\to0$ as $\delta\downarrow0$.

For each $m\ge1$, only finitely many cubes of side $2^{-m}$ meet a fixed ball containing the common supports; all other cell averages vanish. Enumerate all these cells at all levels by first increasing $m$ and then lexicographic order of their integer coordinates. Each cell-average coefficient $a_j(k)$ is a bounded real sequence, with bound $M$ divided by that cell's volume. Set $S_0=\mathbb N$ and initialize $k_0=0$. Recursively, at stage $m\ge1$, partition the bounded ranges of the first $m$ coefficients into finitely many half-open dyadic bins of width $2^{-m}$, adding an endpoint bin if necessary. Among the finitely many vector bins containing infinitely many indices in $S_{m-1}$, take the lexicographically first; let $S_m$ be exactly that infinite set of indices. The finite pigeonhole principle guarantees existence and the specified order makes the rule unique. Then let $k_m$ be the least member of $S_m$ larger than $k_{m-1}$; such a member exists because $S_m$ is infinite. This deterministic successor rule and initial pair $(S_0,k_0)$ define the sequence recursively by [F3], with no dependent-choice instance. For fixed $j$ and $m\ge j$, all selected indices $k_q$ with $q\ge m$ lie in $S_m$, so their $j$th coefficients differ by at most $2^{-m}$. Consequently every coefficient converges and, at each fixed cell level $\ell$, $(A_{2^{-\ell}}v_{k_m})_m$ is Cauchy in $L^1$, being a finite weighted sum of these coefficients.

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a cell level $\ell$ for which $2^n\omega(\sqrt n2^{-\ell})<\varepsilon/3$, using step 1.1. For sufficiently large $a,b$, step 1.2 gives $\|A_{2^{-\ell}}v_{k_a}-A_{2^{-\ell}}v_{k_b}\|_1<\varepsilon/3$. The two approximation errors from step 1.1 then show $\|v_{k_a}-v_{k_b}\|_1<\varepsilon$. Thus the subsequence is Cauchy.

For completeness at exactly the stated axiom strength, choose representatives of this countable sequence by [A1]. Select a further subsequence $g_j$ with $\|g_{j+1}-g_j\|_1<2^{-j}$, always choosing the least sufficiently late index, which exists by the Cauchy property. By [F1], $\sum_j|g_{j+1}-g_j|$ is integrable and finite almost everywhere. Hence $g_j$ has a measurable almost-everywhere limit $g$; moreover $|g|\le|g_1|+\sum_j|g_{j+1}-g_j|$, so $g\in L^1$, and $\|g-g_j\|_1\le\sum_{i\ge j}2^{-i}\to0$. The original Cauchy subsequence also converges to this $L^1$ class by the triangle inequality. This proves the assertion using only [A1].

For coordinate $i$, the unused coordinates contribute $(2r)^{m-1}$, while the measure of endpoint pairs whose interval contains a fixed coordinate value is at most $(2r)^2$. It is a lower semicontinuous extended nonnegative function on $L^1$: each test integral is a continuous linear functional and $\{f:V(f)>a\}$ is the union of its open superlevel sets. By [F2], $V(f)<\infty$ is equivalent to $f\in BV$, in which case $V(f)=TV(f;\Omega)$. For $t>0$ the indicator $\chi_{\{f>t\}}$ lies in $L^1$, since its norm is at most $\|f\|_1/t$, and it is right continuous as an $L^1$-valued function of $t$: if $t_j\downarrow t>0$, its indicators increase to $\chi_{\{f>t\}}$ and their errors tend to zero by monotone convergence. Dyadic right-step approximations therefore make this map Borel measurable. For $t<0$, $t\mapsto\chi_{\{f<t\}}$ is similarly left continuous and Borel. Composition with the lower semicontinuous $V$ shows that both extended level-variation functions are measurable.

By [F1], take smooth strict approximants $u_j$ with $\|u_j-u\|_1<2^{-j}$ and $\int|\nabla u_j|\to TV(u;\Omega)$, passing to a subsequence by least indices if needed. For real numbers $a,b$, the total length of the positive and negative levels at which their signed superlevel or sublevel indicators differ is $|a-b|$. Hence [F3] gives $$\int_0^\infty\|\chi_{\{u_j>t\}}-\chi_{\{u>t\}}\|_1\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0\|\chi_{\{u_j<t\}}-\chi_{\{u<t\}}\|_1\,dt=\|u_j-u\|_1.$$ Sum over $j$ and apply [F3]: for almost every applicable nonzero level, the indicator errors are summable, and in particular the level indicators converge in $L^1$. The lower semicontinuity from step 1.1 gives $V(\chi_{E_t^\pm})\le\liminf_jV(\chi_{\{u_j\gtrless t\}})$ at those levels. Fatou and the smooth coarea identity [F1] consequently give $$\int_0^\infty V(\chi_{E_t^+})\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0V(\chi_{E_t^-})\,dt\le\liminf_j\int_\Omega|\nabla u_j|\,dx=TV(u;\Omega).$$ The integral is finite, so its integrands are finite almost everywhere; [F2] then proves the stated almost-everywhere finite-perimeter assertion.

Each smaller graph base is bounded and its Lipschitz constant finite, so [F2] gives finite Radon surface measure on that patch and $\mathcal H^{n-1}(\partial\Omega)<\infty$. In each chart [F1] defines a local trace and bounds its surface $L^1$ norm, using [F2], by a chart constant times $\|u\|_1+|Du|(\Omega)$. On overlaps these local traces agree by [F1]. Consequently they define one class $Tu\in L^1(\partial\Omega,\mathcal H^{n-1})$ with $\|Tu\|_1\le C(\|u\|_1+TV(u;\Omega))$. Linearity follows locally from [F1], hence globally.

Construct a finite smooth partition equal to one on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, subordinate to the boundary charts and the interior open set $\Omega$: by [F5] this compact set is covered by finitely many balls with doubled closures in those open sets; take the bumps in [F3], and divide them by their positive sum near $\overline\Omega$. Multiply by one further smooth cutoff supported where the sum is positive and equal to one near $\overline\Omega$. First take $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^n)$ and apply the local Green identity [F1] to each chart-supported field $\eta_j\phi$. For the interior-supported field the defining distributional identity applies. Sum the identities. Since $\sum_j\eta_j=1$ and $\sum_j\nabla\eta_j=0$ near $\overline\Omega$, the interior and boundary sums are exactly $$\int_\Omega u\operatorname{div}\phi=-\int_\Omega\phi\cdot dDu+\int_{\partial\Omega}Tu\,\phi\cdot\nu\,d\mathcal H^{n-1}.$$ For an arbitrary $\phi\in C_c^1$, use [F7] to approximate $\phi$ and its first derivatives uniformly by compactly supported smooth fields; finite variation and $Tu\in L^1$ pass every term to the limit.

Extend each coordinate of $Du$ by zero from $\Omega$ to $\mathbb R^n$. It is a finite signed Radon measure: compact inner approximation can be performed inside $\Omega$, and outer approximation in the ambient space follows by applying that inner approximation to the complement and using finiteness. For each coordinate $i$, the boundary density $f_i:=Tu\,
u_i$ is integrable because $Tu\in L^1$ and $|
u_i|\le1$. By [F6], $f_i\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\partial\Omega}$ is a finite signed Radon measure; this verifies the required weighted-measure regularity, not just its finiteness. Thus their difference $\mu=i_\#Du-Tu\,
u\mathcal H^{n-1}|_{\partial\Omega}$ is a finite Radon vector measure by [F4]. The formula in step 2.1 says exactly that $D\widetilde u=\mu$, so $\widetilde u\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$.

The two summands defining $\mu$ in step 3.1 are supported on the disjoint Borel sets $\Omega$ and $\partial\Omega$. The partition definition of variation therefore gives the sum of their variations. For a unit measurable vector density $
u$ and scalar density $Tu$, the boundary variation is $|Tu|\mathcal H^{n-1}$: the triangle inequality gives the upper bound, and a finite partition of the unit sphere into pieces of diameter below $\epsilon$, applied to the direction $\operatorname{sgn}(Tu)
u$, gives the lower bound $(1-\epsilon)|Tu|\mathcal H^{n-1}$ by projection; let $\epsilon\downarrow0$. Hence $TV(\widetilde u)=TV(u;\Omega)+\|Tu\|_1$. Step 1.1 gives the asserted bound. If another trace satisfied the Green identity, their difference times $
u\mathcal H^{n-1}$ would integrate to zero on all smooth tests, hence be zero by [F3]; the same variation calculation gives equality of the trace classes.

A bounded open set with finite boundary is a finite disjoint union of bounded intervals. Use the one-sided endpoint construction in [F1] on each of their finitely many endpoints. citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, meaning a bounded open set whose boundary has a finite cover by Lipschitz graph neighborhoods with $\Omega$ on one side of each graph. The zero-extension map is bounded from $BV(\Omega)$ to $BV(\mathbb R^n)$, with support in $\overline\Omega$, and there is a finite $C_\Omega$ such that $$\|\widetilde u\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^n)}+TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^n)\le C_\Omega\bigl(\|u\|_{L^1(\Omega)}+TV(u;\Omega)\bigr)$$ for every $u\in BV(\Omega)$. For every $v\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ and $h\in\mathbb R^n$, $$\|v(\cdot+h)-v\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^n)}\le |h|TV(v;\mathbb R^n).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(v_k)$ be a sequence in real $L^1(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\sup_k\|v_k\|_1<\infty$, all zero almost everywhere outside one bounded set. If $\lim_{r\downarrow0}\sup_{k,\ |h|\le r}\|v_k(\cdot+h)-v_k\|_1=0$, then a subsequence converges in $L^1(\mathbb R^n)$. This assertion does not require Dependent Choice.

For every open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and real-valued $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $$TV(u;\Omega)=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^n),\ |\varphi(x)|\le1\right\}.$$ If $u_k,u\in BV(\Omega)$ are real-valued and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$, then $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. In addition, assuming Countable Choice, for any real-valued $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ the displayed supremum is finite if and only if $u\in BV(\Omega)$, with equality to $TV(u;\Omega)$; under the same assumption, an $L^1$ limit of real-valued BV functions with bounded liminf total variation belongs to $BV(\Omega)$ and satisfies the same lower-semicontinuity inequality.

derivations.claim: For $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(\Omega)$ with all functions in $BV(\Omega)$, each compactly supported smooth unit test field has $\int u\operatorname{div}\phi=\lim_k\int u_k\operatorname{div}\phi\le\liminf_kTV(u_k;\Omega)$. Taking the supremum using [F3] proves the lower-semicontinuity assertion. If only $u\in L^1$ is initially known and that liminf is finite, the Countable Choice characterization in [F3] also proves $u\in BV$.

Extend every $u_k$ by zero. By [F1], the functions $v_k=\widetilde u_k$ have support in the bounded set $\overline\Omega$, satisfy $\sup_k\|v_k\|_1\le M$, and have $TV(v_k;\mathbb R^n)\le C_\Omega M$. Their translation differences are at most $|h|C_\Omega M$, uniformly in $k$. Hence [F2] gives a subsequence $v_{k_j}\to v$ in $L^1(\mathbb R^n)$. Restriction yields $u_{k_j}\to u=v|_\Omega$ in $L^1(\Omega)$. The variations in $\Omega$ are bounded by $M$, so step 1.1 and [F3] prove $u\in BV(\Omega)$ and $TV(u;\Omega)\le\liminf_jTV(u_{k_j};\Omega)$. This proves the full compactness conclusion.

derivations.claim: The empty domain gives the inequality with both sides zero, so assume $\Omega\ne\varnothing$. Its openness and nonemptiness give an open box with positive side lengths contained in $\Omega$, and its boundedness puts $\Omega$ inside a bounded box; [F5] therefore gives $0<|\Omega|<\infty$. For $m=\min(|E|,|\Omega\setminus E|)$, take $A$ to be the smaller side. Its indicator is BV: the distributional derivative of the constant function $1$ in $\Omega$ is zero, so $D\chi_{\Omega\setminus E}=-D\chi_E$ and both sides have the same relative perimeter $P$. Its zero extension has $L^{n/(n-1)}$ norm $m^a$. By [F1] and [F4], $m^a\le C(m+P)$ for a fixed $C\ge1$ depending only on $\Omega$. If $0<m\le\delta=(2C)^{-n}$, then $Cm\le m^a/2$, so $m^a\le2CP$. For $m=0$ the conclusion is immediate.

Among sets with $\delta\le|E|\le|\Omega|-\delta$, the relative perimeters have a positive lower bound, unless that family is empty. Otherwise, if the infimum were zero, Countable Choice would select a sequence $E_j$ in this family with $P(E_j;\Omega)<1/j$. Its indicators are uniformly BV-bounded. By [F2], a subsequence converges in $L^1(\Omega)$ to $v\in BV(\Omega)$ with $TV(v;\Omega)=0$. The distance from $v(x)$ to $\{0,1\}$ is bounded by $|v(x)-\chi_{E_j}(x)|$ for every $j$, so its integral is zero by $L^1$ convergence; hence $v$ is an indicator almost everywhere. Its volume lies in $[\delta,|\Omega|-\delta]$ by $L^1$ convergence. But its zero variation makes every coordinate distributional derivative zero, so [F3] makes $v$ constant almost everywhere. An indicator constant must be zero or one, contradicting the volume bounds. This proves a positive lower bound $b_\Omega$ whenever the family is nonempty.

In the remaining case $m\ge\delta$, both side volumes meet the bounds in step 2.1, so $P\ge b_\Omega$ and $m^a\le(|\Omega|/2)^a\le(|\Omega|/2)^ab_\Omega^{-1}P$. Combine this constant with $2C$ from step 1.1. If the intermediate-volume family is empty, step 1.1 already covers every set. Thus a finite domain constant gives the asserted inequality for every finite-perimeter $E$.
